translations.text: After Saul died, David returned from defeating the Amalekites and stayed in Ziklag for two days.
On the third day, a man came from Saul’s camp with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. When he came to David, he fell to the ground and bowed before him.
David asked him, “Where have you come from?” He answered, “I escaped from the camp of Israel.”
David said to him, “What happened? Tell me.” He answered, “The people fled from the battle, and many of the people fell. Saul and his son Jonathan are dead.”
David said to the young man, “Tell me how Saul and his son Jonathan died.”
The young man said to him, “I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul, leaning on his spear. The chariots and horsemen had overtaken him.
He turned around, saw me, and called to me. I answered, ‘Here I am.’
He asked me, ‘Who are you?’ I told him, ‘I am an Amalekite.’
He said to me, ‘Stand over me and kill me, because convulsions have seized me, yet my life is still fully in me.’
So I stood over him and killed him, because I knew he would not survive his fall. I took the crown that was on his head and the bracelet that was on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord.”
David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and so did all the men who were with him.
They mourned, wept, and fasted until evening for Saul, for his son Jonathan, for the LORD’s people, and for the Israelites who had fallen by the sword.
David asked the young man who had brought him the news, “Where are you from?” He answered, “I am the son of an Amalekite immigrant.”
David said to him, “How were you not afraid to stretch out your hand to destroy the LORD’s anointed?”
David called one of the young men and said to him, “Come forward and strike him down.” He came forward, attacked him, and struck him, and he died.
David said to him, “Your blood is on your own head, because your own mouth testified against you when you said, ‘I killed the LORD’s anointed.’”
David sang this lament over Saul and his son Jonathan.
He ordered that the people of Judah be taught the Bow. It is written in the Book of Jashar:
O glory of Israel! The slain lie on your heights! How the mighty have fallen!
Do not tell it in Gath or announce it in the streets of Ashkelon, so that the daughters of the Philistines will not rejoice and the daughters of the uncircumcised will not celebrate.
Mountains of Gilboa, may there be neither dew nor rain upon you, nor fields of offerings! For there the shield of the mighty was broken—the shield of Saul, which was anointed with oil.
From the blood of the slain and the fat of the mighty, Jonathan’s bow did not turn back, and Saul’s sword did not return empty.
Saul and Jonathan, loved and pleasant in their lives, were not parted in their deaths. They were swifter than eagles and stronger than lions.
Daughters of Israel, weep for Saul, who clothed you in scarlet over dyed fabrics and adorned your clothing with ornaments of gold.
How the mighty have fallen in the midst of battle! Jonathan lies slain on your heights!
I grieve for you, my brother Jonathan. You were very dear to me. Your love for me was more extraordinary than the love of women.
How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!
After this, David consulted the Lord and asked, “Should I go up to one of the towns of Judah?” The Lord told him, “Go up.” David asked, “Where should I go?” He said, “To Hebron.”
David went up there with his two wives, Ahinoam from Jezreel and Abigail, the wife of Nabal the Carmelite.
David and his men went up together, along with the members of his household, and they settled in Hebron.
The men of Judah came there to anoint David as king over the house of Judah. They informed David, saying, “The men of Jabesh-gilead buried Saul.”
David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and told them, “May you be blessed by the Lord, because you showed this kindness to your master Saul by burying him.
Now may the Lord show you kindness and faithfulness. I too will show you kindness because you have done this.
Now strengthen your hands and be brave, for your master Saul is dead, and the people of Judah have anointed me to reign over them.”
Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul’s army, took Ish-bosheth son of Saul and brought him across to Mahanaim.
He made him king over Gilead, Geshur, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel.
Ish-bosheth son of Saul was forty years old when he became king over Israel, and he reigned for two years. The house of Judah, however, followed David.
The length of time that King David reigned in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.
Abner son of Ner and the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon.
Joab son of Zeruiah and David’s men went out and met them, the young men, together at Gibeon. These young men sat on one side, and those young men on the other.
Abner said to Joab, “Let the young men get up and hold a contest before us.” Joab said, “Let them get up.”
They got up and crossed over, twelve men from Benjamin belonging to Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve of David’s men.
Each seized his opponent by the head and thrust his sword into his opponent’s side, and they fell together. That place, which is in Gibeon, was called Helkath-hazzurim.
The battle was very fierce that day, and Abner and the men of Israel were defeated by David’s servants.
The three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Asahel was as swift on his feet as one of the gazelles in the wilderness.
Asahel pursued Abner, without turning aside to the right or to the left as he followed him.
Abner looked behind him and asked, “Is that you, Asahel?” He answered, “It is.”
Abner told him, “Turn aside to your right or your left, seize one of the young men, and take his weapons for yourself.” But Asahel refused to turn aside from pursuing him.
Abner again told Asahel to turn aside from pursuing him. He said, “Stop following me, or I will strike you down to the ground. How could I then lift my face and look at your brother Joab?”

But he refused to turn aside. Abner struck him in the chest with the butt of his spear, and it came out through his back. He fell there and died on the spot. Everyone who came to the place where Asahel had fallen stopped.
Joab and Abishai set out in pursuit of Abner. The sun was setting when they reached the hill of Ammah, opposite Giah, on the road to the wilderness of Gibeon.
The Benjaminites gathered behind Abner, formed a single company, and took their stand on top of a hill.
Abner called to Joab and said, “Will the sword keep killing forever? Don’t you know that this will end in bitterness? How long will you wait before telling the men to stop pursuing their brothers?”
Joab said, “As the Lord lives, if you had not spoken, I would certainly have called off the men in the morning, each from pursuing his brother.”
Joab blew the trumpet, and all the men stopped. They no longer pursued Israel, and they stopped fighting.
Abner and his men traveled through the wilderness all that night. They crossed the Jordan, went toward Geshur, and came to Mahanaim.
Joab turned back from pursuing Abner. All the troops assembled, and those of David’s men who had been struck down were counted: twelve men, and Asahel was dead.
David’s men killed three hundred and sixty men from Benjamin and from Abner’s men.
They took Asahel and buried him in his father’s tomb in Bethlehem. Joab and his companions traveled all night, and day dawned on them at Hebron.
There was war between the house of Saul and the house of David. David grew stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker.
Sons were born to David in Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel.
His second was Caleb, by Abigail, the wife of Nabal of Carmel; and the third was Absalom, the son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur.
The fourth was Adonijah, the son of Haggith, and the fifth was Shephatiah, the son of Abital.
The sixth was Ithream, by Eglah, David’s wife. These were born to David in Hebron.
While there was war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner was strengthening his position in the house of Saul.
Saul had a concubine named Rizpah, daughter of Anah. Ish-bosheth said to Abner, “Why have you slept with my father’s concubine?”

Abner was very angry at Ish-bosheth’s words. Abner said, “Am I a dog’s head belonging to Judah today? I have shown kindness to the house of Saul your father, to his brothers, and to his friends, and I have not handed you over to David. Yet today you accuse me of wrongdoing involving a woman!
May God do this to Abner, and more besides, if I do not do for David just as the LORD has said to him:
to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and establish David’s throne over Israel and Judah, from Dan to Beersheba.”
Ish-bosheth could not say another word in reply to Abner, because he was afraid of him.
Abner sent messengers to David, saying, “What is the land? Make your covenant with me, and I will be on your side to bring all Israel over to you.”
David said, “Good. I will make a covenant with you. But I ask one thing of you: you must not see my face unless you bring Michal, Saul’s daughter, with you.”
David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth son of Saul and said to him, “Give me my wife, whom I betrothed to myself with two hundred Philistine foreskins.”
Ish-bosheth sent for her and took her away from her husband, Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim.
Her husband went along, walking and weeping behind her as far as Bahurim. Abner said to him, “Go back,” and he went back.
Abner spoke to the elders of Israel and said to them, “For some time you have wanted David to reign over you.
Now do so, because the LORD has said concerning David, ‘Through David my servant I will save my people Israel from the power of the Philistines and from the power of all their enemies.’”
Abner also spoke before the Benjaminites. Then Abner went to speak before David in Hebron, as Israel and the whole house of Benjamin approved.
Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty men. David prepared a great feast for Abner and the twenty men with him.

Abner said to David, “I will rise and go and gather all Israel to my lord the king. They will make a covenant with you, and you will reign over all that your heart desires.” David sent Abner away, and he went in peace.
David’s men and Joab returned from a raid, bringing a great deal of plunder with them. Abner was no longer with David in Hebron, because David had sent him away, and he had gone in peace.
Joab and all the troops with him arrived, and Joab was told, “Abner son of Ner came to King David, and he sent him away, and he went in peace.”
Joab came to King David and said to him, “What have you done? Abner came to you! Why did you send him away and let him leave you?
Don’t you know that Abner son of Ner came to deceive you, to learn your movements, and to find out everything you are doing?”
Joab left David and sent messengers after Abner. They brought him back from the cistern of Sirah, but David did not know.
When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside inside the gateway to speak with him privately. There he struck him in the abdomen, and he died, in revenge for the blood of Joab’s brother Asahel.
Afterward David heard about it and said, “I and my kingdom are forever innocent before the Lord of the blood of Abner son of Ner.

May it fall on Joab’s head and on his father’s entire household. May Joab’s household never lack someone with a discharge, someone with leprosy, someone who holds a spindle, someone who falls by the sword, or someone who lacks bread.”
Joab and his brother Abishai killed Abner because he had killed their brother Asahel in battle at Gibeon.
David said to Joab and all the people with him, “Tear your clothes, wrap yourselves in sackcloth, and dance before Abner.” King David and all the people walked behind the bier.
They buried Abner in Hebron. The king raised his voice and wept at Abner’s grave, and all the people wept.
The king mourned for Abner and said, “Did Abner die as Nabal died?”
Your hands were not bound, and your feet were not brought into chains. You fell as someone falls before wicked men. And all the people wept for him again.
All the people urged David to eat bread while it was still daylight, but David swore, “May God do this to me, and more besides, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun sets.”
All the people took notice and were pleased. Everything the king did was pleasing in the eyes of all the people.
That day all the people and all Israel knew that the killing of Abner son of Ner had not come from the king.
The king said, “Don’t you know that a great leader has fallen today in Israel?
Today I am afraid, and I, the king, have seen that these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too harsh for me. May the Lord repay the evildoer according to his evil.”
When Ish-bosheth son of Saul heard that Abner had died in Hebron, his hands grew weak, and all Israel was troubled.

Saul’s son had two men who commanded raiding bands. One was named Baanah and the other Rechab. They were sons of Rimmon from Beeroth, of the tribe of Benjamin, for Beeroth too was counted as belonging to Benjamin.
The Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have lived there as resident foreigners to this day.

Jonathan son of Saul had a son whose feet were disabled. He was five years old when news about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel. His nurse picked him up and fled, but as she hurried to escape, he fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.
Rechab and Baanah, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, went to Ish-bosheth’s house in the heat of the day while he was taking his midday rest.
They entered the house and took some grains of wheat. Rechab and his brother Baanah struck him in the abdomen and escaped.
They entered the house while he was sleeping on his bed in his bedroom. They struck him, killed him, and took his head. Then they traveled along the Arabah road all night.

They brought Ish-bosheth’s head to David at Hebron and said to King David, “Here is the head of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life. Today the Lord will give our lord the king vengeance on Saul and his descendants.”
David answered Rechab and his brother Baanah, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and said, “As the Lord lives, who has rescued my life from every trouble,
the man who told me, ‘Look, Saul is dead,’ seemed to me like a bearer of good news. Yet I seized him and killed him at Ziklag instead of giving him a reward for the news.
And wicked men killed a man in his own house, on his bed. Now I will demand an accounting for his blood from your hands and wipe you from the earth.
David sent the young men, and they killed them, cut off their hands and feet, and hung them on the hill in Hebron. They took Ish-bosheth’s head and buried it in Abner’s tomb in Hebron.
All the tribes of the house of Israel came to David at Hebron and said to him, “Look, we are your own flesh and bone.

Even in the past, when Saul was king over us, you were the one who led Israel out and brought them in. The Lord said to you, ‘You will shepherd my people Israel, and you will be ruler over my people Israel.’”
All the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron. King David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the Lord, and they anointed David as king over Israel.
David was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned for forty years.
In Hebron he reigned over the house of Judah for seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned for thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.

King David and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land. They said to David, “You will not enter here unless you remove the blind and the lame.” They said, “David will not enter here.”
David captured the fortress of Zion, which is the City of David.

David said that day, “Whoever strikes the Jebusites and approaches the blind and the lame through the water channel—David’s soul hates them.” That is why people say, “The blind and the lame shall not enter the house.”
David lived in the fortress, that is, Zion, and called it the City of David. David built around it on the inside.
David grew greater and greater, and the Lord, his God of hosts, was with him.
Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, along with cedar wood, woodworkers, and stonemasons for the walls, and they built a house for David.
David knew that the Lord had established him as king over Israel and that his kingdom had been exalted over his people Israel.
David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem after he came from Hebron, and more sons and daughters were born to David.
These are the names of the sons born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, [?], Nathan, and Solomon.
And Ibhar [?], Elisha, Nepheg, and Japhia [?].
And Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.
The Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, and all the Philistines went up to seek David. David heard about it and went down to the fortress.
The Philistines came and camped in the Valley of the Giants.
David inquired of the Lord, saying, “Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you deliver them into my hands?” The Lord said to him, “Go up, because I will deliver them into your hands.”
David came to Baal-perazim and defeated them there. David said, “The Lord has broken through his enemies before me like a breakthrough of water.” Therefore he named that place Baal-perazim.
They abandoned their idols there, and David and his men carried them away.
The Philistines came up again and camped in the Valley of the Giants.
David inquired of the Lord, and the Lord said to him, “Do not go up. Instead, circle around behind them and come against them opposite Bachim.
When you hear the sound of marching on the summit of the mountain of Bachim, then act boldly, because then the Lord will go out before you to strike the Philistine camp.”
David did just as the Lord had commanded him, and he defeated the Philistines from Geba as far as the entrance to Geder.
David again gathered all the troops of Israel, thirty thousand men.

David set out with all the people who were with him from among the men of Judah, and he went to Geba to bring up from there the ark of God, over which the name of the Lord of hosts, who sits enthroned above the cherubim, was invoked.
They placed the ark of God on a new cart and brought it from Abinadab’s house on the hill. Uzzah and Ahio, Abinadab’s sons, were driving the cart from behind.
They brought the ark of God from Abinadab’s house in Gibeah, and Ahio walked ahead of the ark.
David and the whole house of Israel were celebrating before the Lord with instruments of cedar and cypress wood, with lyres and harps, with drums and [?], and with cymbals.
They came to the prepared threshing floors, and Uzzah reached out his hand toward the ark of the Lord and took hold of it because the oxen had slipped.
The Lord’s anger burned against Uzzah, and the Lord struck him there because he had reached out his hand. He died there beside the ark of God.
David was distressed because the Lord had broken out against Uzzah, and he called that place Perez-uzzah, as it is called to this day.
David was afraid of the Lord that day and said, “How can I bring the ark of the Lord to me?”
David was unwilling to bring the ark of God to himself in the City of David, so David diverted it to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.
The ark of the Lord remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months, and the Lord blessed Obed-edom the Gittite and his entire household.

King David was told, “The Lord has blessed Obed-edom and everything he has because of the ark of the Lord.” So David went and brought the ark of the Lord up from Obed-edom’s house to the City of David with rejoicing.
When those carrying the ark of the Lord had walked six steps, David sacrificed fattened oxen.
David was praising the Lord with all his strength, and David was wearing a linen ephod.
David and all Israel were bringing up the ark of the Lord with shouts of joy and the sound of the trumpet.

The ark of the Lord was at David’s house, and Michal, Saul’s daughter, looked out through the window. She saw King David rejoicing and celebrating before the ark of the Lord, and she despised him in her heart.
They brought in the ark of the Lord and set it inside the tent David had pitched for it. David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the Lord.
When David had finished offering the burnt offerings and peace offerings to the Lord, he blessed the people in the name of the Lord Almighty.
He distributed to all the people, to the whole assembly of Israel, both men and women, one loaf of bread, one portion of meat, and one [?] each. Then all the people went home, each to his own house.

David turned to go home, and Michal, Saul’s daughter, came out to meet him. She said, “How dignified the king of Israel was today, exposing himself today before the eyes of his servants’ slave women! You exposed yourself shamelessly like one of the worthless men!”

David said to Michal, “It was before the Lord, who chose me rather than your father or anyone in his household and appointed me ruler over the Lord’s people, over Israel. It was for him that I made merry before the Lord.
I will make myself even more insignificant than this and be lowly in my own eyes. But among the slave women you spoke of, I will be honored.”
Michal, Saul’s daughter, had no child until the day she died.
When the king was living in his house and the Lord had given him rest from all his enemies,
the king said to Nathan the prophet, “Look, I am living in a house of cedar, while the ark of God remains inside curtains.”
Nathan said to the king, “Do everything you have in mind, for the Lord is with you.”
That very night the word of the Lord came to Nathan the prophet, saying:
“Go and tell my servant David, ‘This is what the Lord says: You shall not build me a house to live in.
For I have not lived in a house from the day I brought the Israelites up from the land of Egypt until today. Instead, I have moved about in tents.

Wherever I moved about among all the Israelites, did I ever say a word to any of the tribes of Israel whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel? Did I ever say, “Why have you not built me a house of cedar?”
Now say this to my servant David: This is what the Lord Almighty says: I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to be ruler over my people Israel.
I have been with you wherever you went, and I have destroyed all your enemies before you. I will make your name great, like the names of the great ones on earth.

I will make a place for my people Israel, plant them, and settle them peacefully in their own place. They will no longer be disturbed, and wicked people will no longer enslave them as they did before.
From the day I appointed you judge over my people Israel, I have given you rest from all your enemies. The Lord has told you that the Lord will make a house for you.
When your days are complete and you lie down with your ancestors, I will raise up your offspring after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom.
He will build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
I will be his father, and he will be my son. When he does wrong, I will discipline him with a human rod and with blows such as people give.
But I will not take my faithful love away from him as I took it away from Saul, who was before you and whom I removed from my presence.
Your house and your kingdom will be secure before me forever, and your throne will be established before me forever.
Nathan the prophet told David all these words and this entire vision.
King David came and sat before the Lord and said, “Who am I, Lord God, and what is my house, that you have brought me this far?
This was a small thing in your eyes, Lord God, for you have spoken about your servant’s house far into the future. This is the instruction for mankind, Lord God.
What more can your servant David say to you? You yourself know your servant, Lord God.
For the sake of your words and according to your own heart, you have done all this great work to make it known to your servant.
Therefore you are great, Lord God, for there is no one like you, and there is no God besides you, according to all we have heard with our own ears.

Who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem as a people for himself, to make a name for himself, and to perform great deeds and marvelous sights for them on earth, as he did long ago for your people whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt, the people whose God you are?
You established your people Israel for yourself to be your people forever, and you, Lord, became their God.
Now, Lord God, confirm forever the word you have spoken concerning your servant and his house, and do as you have said.
May your name be great forever, as you have said, mighty Lord, God of Israel. May the house of your servant David be established before you forever.
For you, mighty Lord, God of Israel, have revealed this to your servant, saying, ‘I will build you a house.’ Therefore your servant has resolved in his heart to pray this prayer before you.
Now, Lord God, you are God. May your words prove true, for you have spoken this good promise concerning your servant.
Now begin and bless the house of your servant, so that it may remain before you forever. For you, Lord God, have spoken, and through your blessing may your servant’s house be blessed forever.”
After this, David struck the Philistines and defeated them, and David took Ramath-gamma from the Philistines.

He struck the Moabites and measured them with ropes, making them lie down on the ground. He measured two rope lengths for those to be killed and one full rope length for those to be kept alive. The Moabites became David’s subjects and brought tribute.
David struck Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, when he went to restore his control at the Euphrates River.
David destroyed seventeen hundred of his chariots and twenty thousand foot soldiers. David disabled all the chariots but spared a hundred of them.
Edom and Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, and David struck down twenty-two thousand in Edom.
David stationed garrisons in Edom and Damascus, and the Edomites became David’s servants, bringing tribute. The Lord delivered David wherever he went.
David took the gold shields carried by Hadadezer’s servants, and King David took a very large quantity of bronze and brought them to Jerusalem.
From Tebah and Berothai, the towns of Hadadezer.
Toi king of Hamath heard that David had defeated Hadadezer’s entire army.

Toi sent his son Joram to King David to ask about his well-being and congratulate him because he had fought Hadadezer and defeated him, for Hadadezer was a warlike man. Joram son of Toi took silver vessels, gold vessels, and bronze vessels with him and brought them to David.
King David also dedicated these to the Lord, along with the silver and gold he had dedicated from all the nations he had subdued:
from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, the Amalekites, and the territory ruled by Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah.
David fought a battle there when he returned after defeating Edom in the Valley of Salt, killing eighteen thousand.
David appointed governors throughout Edom, and all the Edomites became David’s servants. The Lord delivered David wherever he went.
David reigned over all Israel, administering justice and righteousness for all his people.
Joab son of Zeruiah commanded the army, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder.
Zadok son of Ahitub the Gilonite and Abiathar son of Ahimelech were priests, and Seraiah was the scribe.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was in charge of the nobles and the soldiers, and David’s sons were high officials.
David said, “Is there still anyone left from the house of Saul, so that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
Saul’s household had a servant named Ziba. They summoned him to David, and the king said to him, “Are you Ziba?” He answered, “I am your servant.”
The king said to him, “Is there anyone still left from Saul’s household to whom I can show mercy for God’s sake?” Ziba said to the king, “Jonathan still has a son living, whose feet are disabled.”
The king asked him, “Where is he?” Ziba said to the king, “He is at the house of Machir son of Gamal, in Lo-debar.”
The king sent for him and brought him from the house of Machir son of Gamal in Lo-debar.
Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David, fell facedown, and bowed. David said to him, “Mephibosheth!” He answered, “Your servant has come.”

David said to him, “Do not be afraid, because I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will restore to you all the fields of your father Saul, and you will always eat at my table.”
He bowed and said, “What is your servant worth, that you have taken notice of me, a dead dog?”
The king summoned Ziba and said to him, “Everything that belonged to Saul and his entire household I have given to your master’s son.

You, your sons, and your servants shall work the land for him and bring in food for your master’s son to eat. But Mephibosheth, your master’s son, will always eat at my table.” Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Ziba said to the king, “Your servant will do everything my lord the king has commanded his servant.” Mephibosheth ate at the king’s table like one of the king’s sons.
Mephibosheth had a young son named Micah. Everyone living in Ziba’s household became Mephibosheth’s servants.
Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem because he always ate at the king’s table. Both his feet were disabled.
Afterward, the king of the Ammonites died, and his son Hanun reigned in his place.

David said, “I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me.” David sent his servants to comfort him over his father, and David’s servants came to the land of the Ammonites.

The Ammonite officials said to their lord Hanun, “Do you think David is honoring your father by sending you men to comfort you? Hasn’t David sent his servants to you to spy out the city, investigate it, and overthrow it?”
Hanun seized David’s servants, shaved off half their beards, cut their tunics with arrows as far as their buttocks, and sent them away.
David was told, and he sent men to meet them, because the men were deeply ashamed. The king said to them, “Stay in Jericho until your beards grow back; then return.”

The Ammonites saw that they had wronged David, so they sent and hired twenty thousand foot soldiers from Edom of Rehob and Edom of Zobah, a thousand men from the king of Maacah, and twelve thousand foot soldiers from Ish-tob.
When David heard this, he sent Joab and the entire army of warriors.
The Ammonites came out and drew up their battle line at the entrance to the gate, while those from Edom of Rehob, Edom of Zobah, Ish-tob, and Maacah were by themselves in the open field.
Joab saw that the battle was arrayed against him both in front and behind. He selected men from all the chosen men of Israel and drew them up against Edom.
He entrusted the rest of the troops to his brother Abishai, who drew them up against the Ammonites.
He said to his brother Abishai, “If Edom proves too strong for me, come to my aid. If the Ammonites prove too strong for you, I will come and help you.
Let us be strong and take our stand for our people and for the cities of our God. May the Lord do what is good in his eyes.”
Joab and the troops with him advanced to fight Edom, and they fled before him.
When the Ammonites saw that Edom had fled, they too fled before Abishai and entered the city. Joab turned back from the Ammonites and went to Jerusalem.
When Edom saw that they had been defeated before Israel, they gathered together.
Hadadezer sent and brought out the Edomites who were beyond the River. They came to Helam, with Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer’s army, leading them.

David was informed, and he gathered all Israel. They crossed the Jordan and came to Helam, with Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer’s army, leading them. Edom drew up its battle line against Israel, and David fought Edom.

Edom fled before Israel, and David killed seventeen hundred chariot warriors, four thousand horsemen, and many other men from Edom. He also struck Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer’s army, and he died there.
When all Hadadezer’s servants saw that they had been defeated before the Israelites, they made peace with Israel and served them. Edom was afraid to help the Ammonites again.
At the turn of the year, at the time when the king goes out, David sent Joab, his servants with him, and all Israel. They camped against Rabbah, while David remained in Jerusalem.
Toward evening David got up from his bed and walked about on the roof of his royal palace. He saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful.
David sent and inquired about the woman. They said, “This is Bathsheba, the daughter of Ahinoam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite.”
David sent a messenger and had her brought to him. She came to him, and he slept with her, after she had bathed to cleanse herself from her menstrual impurity. Then she returned to her house.
The woman became pregnant. She sent word to David and told him, “I am pregnant.”
David sent word to Joab, saying, “Send me Uriah the Hittite.” So Joab sent Uriah the Hittite to David.
Uriah came to David, and David asked Uriah about Joab, the people, and the war.
David said to Uriah, “Go down to your house and wash your feet.” Uriah went out of the king’s house, and a gift from the king followed him.
Uriah slept at the king’s gate beside all his master’s servants and did not go down to his house.
David was told that Uriah had not gone down to his house. David said to Uriah, “You have just come from a journey. Why did you not go down to your house?”

Uriah said to David, “The ark of the Lord’s covenant, Israel, and Judah are staying in shelters, and my lord Joab and my lord’s servants are camping in the open field. Should I go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife? No! As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do such a thing.”
David said to Uriah, “Stay here today, and tomorrow I will send you away.” So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next.
David invited him, and he ate and drank in his presence and became drunk. In the evening he went out and slept beside his master’s servants, but he did not go down to his house.
In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by Uriah’s hand.
He wrote to him, “Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest fighting, and withdraw from behind him so that he will be struck down and die.”
While Joab was besieging the city, he stationed Uriah in a place where he knew there were strong warriors.
The men of the city came out and fought against Joab. Some of the troops, David’s servants, fell there, and Uriah the Hittite also died.
Joab sent word to David and reported everything that had happened in the battle.
Joab instructed the messenger, saying to him, “When you have finished telling the king everything that happened in the battle,
if the king’s anger rises and he says to you, ‘Why did you go near the city to fight against it? Didn’t you know they would shoot from the wall?

Who killed Abimelech son of Nedubbaal? Wasn’t it a woman who threw a piece of an upper millstone down on him from the wall, so that he died? Why did you go near the wall?’ If he says these things to you, tell him, ‘Your servant Uriah the Hittite also died.’”
The messenger went and told David everything Joab had instructed him to say.
The messenger said to David, “The men overpowered us and came out against us into the open country, but we pressed them back as far as the city gate.
Those stationed on the wall shot at us, and some of your servants died, O king. Your servant Uriah the Hittite also died.”
David said to the messenger, “Tell Joab, ‘Do not be distressed about this. Such things happen in battle, one way or another. Press the attack against the city, capture it, and overthrow it.’”
The wife of Uriah the Hittite heard that her husband had died, and she mourned for her husband.
When her days of mourning had passed, David sent for her and brought her into his house. She became his wife and bore him a son. But what David had done was displeasing to the Lord.
The Lord sent Nathan the prophet to David. He came to him and said, “There were two men in one city, one rich and the other poor.
The rich man had very many sheep and cattle.
The poor man had nothing except one little ewe lamb that he had bought. It lived with him and his children, ate his bread, drank from his cup, and slept in his arms. It was like a daughter to him.

A traveler came to the rich man, but he was unwilling to take any of his own cattle or sheep to prepare for the traveler who had come to him. Instead, he took that poor man’s ewe lamb and prepared it for the traveler who had come to him.”
Then David became angry with the man and said, “As the Lord lives, the man who did this deserves to die!
He must repay four lambs for the one, because he did this and showed no pity.”
Nathan said to David, “You are the man! This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you to reign over my people Israel, and I rescued you from Saul’s hands.

I gave you your master’s daughters and laid your master’s wives in your arms. I gave you the daughters of Israel and Judah. If they were too few, you had only to say so, and I would have added as many again and as many again.

Why have you despised the LORD’s command and done what is evil before the LORD? You killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword and took his wife as your own wife. You killed him with the sword of the Ammonites.
Now the sword will never depart from your house, because you despised me and took the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.’

This is what the Lord says: ‘Look, I am raising up disaster against you from within your own house. I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your companion, and he will sleep with them in the sight of this very sun.
You acted secretly, but I will do this in the sight of all Israel and in broad daylight.’”
David said to Nathan, “I have sinned before the Lord.” Nathan said to David, “The Lord has also taken away your guilt. You will not die.
Nevertheless, because by this deed you have exalted the Lord’s enemies, the son born to you by her will certainly die.”
Nathan went home, and the LORD struck the child whom Uriah the Hittite’s wife had borne to David, and he became seriously ill.
David pleaded with God for the child. David fasted, spent the night fasting, and lay on the ground.
The elders of his household stood beside him to raise him from the ground, but he refused and would not eat with them.

On the seventh day the child died. David’s servants were afraid to tell him that the child had died, for they said, “While the child was alive, we spoke to him, but he would not listen to us. How can we tell him now that the child has died? He might do something harmful.”
When David saw his servants whispering, he realized that the child had died. David asked his servants, “Has the child died?” They answered him, “He has died.”

David got up from the ground, washed, anointed himself, and changed his clothes. He entered the house of the LORD and worshiped. Then he went home and asked for food. They set it before him, and he ate.
His servants said to him, “What is this you have done? While the child was alive, you fasted and pleaded, but when he died, you got up and ate.”
David said to them, “While the child was alive, I fasted and pleaded, because I said, ‘Who knows whether God will have mercy on him and the child will live?’
But now that he has died, why should I fast? Can he come back again? I am going to him, but he cannot come to me.”
David comforted his wife Bathsheba. He went to her and slept with her, and she bore a son and named him Solomon. The LORD loved the child.
He sent for Nathan the prophet, who named him Jedidiah, because the LORD loved him.
Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and captured the royal city.
Joab sent messengers to David and said, “I have fought against Rabbah and have also captured the royal city.
Now gather the rest of the people and come, camp against the city, and capture it. Otherwise I will capture the city myself, and it will be called by my name.”
David gathered all the people, went against Rabbah, fought against it, and captured it.
He took their king’s crown from his head. It weighed a talent of gold and contained precious stones, and it was placed on David’s head. He brought out a very great amount of plunder from the city.

He brought out the people who were in it and put them in iron collars and chains, and made them pass under a measuring line. He did the same to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
After this, Absalom son of David had a sister named Tamar, and Amnon son of David fell in love with her.
Amnon was distressed over his sister Tamar, because she was a virgin, and Amnon could not say anything to her.
Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, the son of David’s brother Shimeah. Jonadab was a very shrewd man.
He said to Amnon, “King’s son, why are you wasting away like this morning after morning? Won’t you tell me?” Amnon said to him, “I am in love with Tamar, the sister of my brother Absalom.”

Jonadab said to him, “Lie down on your bed and pretend to be sick. When your father comes to see you, tell him, ‘Let my sister Tamar come and feed me. Let her make cakes for me where I can watch, and let me eat from her hands.’”
Amnon lay down and pretended to be sick. When the king came to see him, Amnon said to the king, “Let my sister Tamar come to me and make two cakes before my eyes, so that I may eat from her hands.”
David sent word to Tamar, saying, “Go to your brother Amnon and prepare food for him.”
Tamar went to the house of her brother Amnon, who was lying down. She took dough, kneaded it, and made cakes.
She took the cakes and set them before him, but he refused to eat. Amnon said, “Have everyone leave me.” So everyone left him.
Amnon said to Tamar, “Bring the food into the bedroom for me, so I can eat from your hands.” Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them into the bedroom to her brother Amnon.
She brought them to him to eat, but he seized her and said to her, “Come, sleep with me, my sister.”
She said to him, “No, my brother! Do not dishonor me. Such a thing must not be done in Israel.
Where could I carry my disgrace? And you would be regarded as one of the fools in Israel. Now speak to the king; he will not withhold me from you.”
But he would not listen to her. He seized her, overpowered her, slept with her, and dishonored her.
Then Amnon hated her intensely. The hatred he felt for her was greater than the love he had felt for her. Amnon said to her, “Get up and go!”
She said to him, “Now that you have done this great evil to me, are you sending me away?” But he would not listen to her.
He called the young man who served him and said to him, “Put this woman outside, away from me, and shut the door in her face.”
Tamar took ashes and put them on her head. She tore the embroidered robe she was wearing, put her hands on her head, and went away wailing.

Her brother Absalom said to her, “Has your brother Amnon slept with you? Now, my sister, keep quiet. He is your brother. Do not take this matter to heart.” So Tamar stayed in her brother Absalom’s house, devastated.
King David heard about all these things and was deeply distressed.
Absalom said nothing to Amnon, either good or bad, because Absalom hated Amnon for dishonoring his sister Tamar.
When the season came around again, Absalom had sheep shearers at Baal-hazor, near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the king’s sons.
Absalom came to the king and said to him, “Your servant has sheep shearers at work. Let the king and his servants come with your servant.”
He said to him, “No, my son. We should not all go, or we will be a burden to you.” Absalom urged him, but he would not go with him. He did, however, give him his blessing.
Absalom said to him, “Then why should my brother Amnon not go with me?” The king said to him, “Why should he go with you?”
But Absalom urged him, and he sent Amnon and all the king’s sons with him.
Absalom commanded his servants, saying, “When Amnon is cheerful from the wine and I tell you, ‘Strike Amnon,’ kill him. Do not be afraid. I myself have commanded you. Be strong and act like men.”
Absalom’s servants did as Absalom had commanded them. Then all the king’s sons got up, each mounted his mule, and they fled.
While they were still on the road, news reached David that Absalom had killed all the king’s sons and had not left a single one alive.
The king rose, tore his clothes, and lay on the ground. All his servants stood there with their clothes torn.

Jonadab, the son of David’s brother Shimeah, spoke up and said to him, “My lord the king must not think that all the king’s sons are dead. Only Amnon is dead, for Absalom had resolved on this from the day Amnon dishonored his sister Tamar.
So now, my lord the king must not think that all the king’s sons are dead. Only Amnon is dead.”
Absalom fled. The lookout raised his eyes and saw many people coming along the road from the side of the mountain.
Jonadab said to the king, “Look, the king’s sons have arrived! It has happened just as your servant said.”
As he finished speaking, the king’s sons arrived. They raised their voices and wept, and the king and all his servants also wept bitterly.
Absalom fled and went to Talmai son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. David mourned for his son for many days.
Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and he stayed there for three years.
King David stopped pursuing Absalom, because he had been comforted over Amnon's death.
Joab son of Zeruiah knew that King David's heart had turned toward Absalom.

Joab sent to Tekoa and brought a wise woman from there. He said to her, "Act as a mourner and put on mourning clothes. Do not anoint yourself with oil, but be like a woman who has been mourning for someone dead for many days.
Go in to the king and say this to him." Joab prepared the words and put them in her mouth.
The woman from Tekoa came in to the king, fell facedown on the ground, bowed, and said, "Save me, my lord the king!"
The king said to her, "What is wrong?" She said to him, "I am indeed a widow; my husband is dead.
Your servant had two sons. The two of them fought in the countryside, and there was no one to separate them. One overpowered the other and killed him.

Now the whole clan has risen against your servant. They say, 'Hand over the one who killed his brother so that we may kill him for the brother he killed.' They want to destroy the heir and extinguish the ember that remains to me, leaving his father neither a name nor descendants on the face of the earth."
The king said to her, "Go home. I will give orders concerning you."
The woman from Tekoa said to the king, "My lord the king, let this guilt fall on me and my father's household, while the king and his throne remain free of blame."
The king said to her, "Bring me anyone who says anything to you, and he will not approach you again."

She said, "Let my lord the king remember that the LORD your God does not destroy through repeated blood vengeance [?]. Do not let them destroy my son." The king said to her, "As the LORD God lives, not one hair of your son's head will fall to the ground."
The woman said, "May your servant say something to the king?" The king said to her, "Speak."
The woman said to him, "Why have you planned such a thing against God's people? Why have you spoken like someone guilty, O king, when you do not bring back the one you have banished?
We will surely die. We are like water poured onto the ground that cannot be gathered up again. God does not take away life, but devises plans so that no one may wander away from him.
Now I have said this to my lord the king because the people frightened me. Your servant said, 'I will speak to the king.
Perhaps he will rescue his servant from the hands of those who would destroy both me and my son from God's inheritance.'
Your servant said, 'May the word of my lord the king stand firm and be an offering.' For my lord the king is like an angel of God in hearing good and evil. May the LORD your God be with you."
The king answered the woman, "Do not hide anything from me that I ask you." The woman said to him, "Speak, my lord the king."

The king said to her, "Is Joab's hand with you in all this?" The woman answered him, "As you live, my lord the king, I have not turned to the right or to the left from anything my lord the king has said. It was your servant Joab who instructed me, and he put all these words in your servant's mouth.
It was so that you would act on my behalf—it was for that reason that your servant Joab did this. My lord is wise, with the wisdom of God's angels, knowing everything that is in the land."
The king said to Joab, "Look, I have done as you said. Go and bring the young man Absalom to me."

Joab fell facedown on the ground, bowed, and blessed the king. Joab said, "Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your eyes, my lord the king, because the king has done what his servant asked."
Joab set out and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.
The king said, “Let him go to his own house, but he must not appear before me.” So Absalom went to his own house and did not see the king.
There was no man in Israel as highly praised as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, there was no blemish in him.
When he cut the hair of his head—he cut it from time to time because it grew heavy on him—he would weigh the hair of his head: two hundred shekels by the royal weight.
Absalom had three sons and one daughter named Tamar. She too was a beautiful woman.
Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two years without seeing the king.
Absalom sent for Joab so that he could send him to the king, but Joab refused to come. He sent for him a second time, but he still refused to come.
Absalom said to his servants, “Look at Joab’s field beside mine, with wheat or barley in it. Go and set it on fire.” So Absalom’s servants set Joab’s field on fire.
Joab got up and went to Absalom’s house. Joab said to Absalom, “Why did your servants set my field on fire?”

Absalom said to Joab, “Look, I sent for you and asked you to come so that I could send you to the king to say, ‘Why did I come from Geshur? I was better off there.’ Now I want to appear before the king. If I am guilty, let him put me to death.”

Joab came before the king and told him what Absalom had said. The king summoned Absalom, and Absalom came before the king and bowed with his face to the ground before him. Then the king kissed Absalom.
After this, Absalom provided himself with chariots and horsemen and fifty runners who ran ahead of him.

Absalom would get up early and stand beside the king’s gate. Whenever a man had a case to be judged before the king, Absalom would call him over and ask him, “What town are you from?” He would answer, “Your servant is from one of the tribes of Israel.”
Absalom would say to him, “Look, I see that your claims are good and right, but there is no one appointed by the king to hear you.”
Absalom would say, “If only someone would make me a judge in the land! Then everyone with a case or a claim would come to me, and I would rule in his favor.”
Whenever a man stood before him to bow down to him, he would take him by the hand and kiss him.
Absalom did this to all the Israelites who came before the king for judgment. In this way Absalom turned the hearts of all the Israelites toward himself.
After four years, Absalom said to the king, “Let me go to Hebron and fulfill the vow I made to the Lord.
For your servant made a vow while I was living in Geshur and in Edom, saying, ‘If the Lord will indeed bring me back to Jerusalem, I will worship the Lord.’”
The king said to him, “Go in peace.” So he set out and went to Hebron.
Absalom sent spies throughout all the tribes of Israel and commanded them, “When you hear the sound of the trumpet, say, ‘Absalom has become king in Hebron!’”
Two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom. They went innocently, knowing nothing about it.

Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counselor, and brought him from his town, Giloh, while he was offering sacrifices. The rebellion kept growing stronger, and the people supporting Absalom increased greatly.
A messenger came to David and told him, “The hearts of the Israelites are united behind Absalom.”

David said to all his servants who were with him in Jerusalem, “Get up! Let us flee, or we will not be able to escape Absalom. Let us leave quickly, or he may hurry and overtake us, bring disaster on us, and put the city to the sword.”
The king’s servants said to the king, “Whatever you wish, our lord the king, your servants will do.”
The king went out, with his entire household following him. The king left ten women, his concubines, to look after his house.
The king went out, with all the people following him, and they stopped some distance away.
All his servants passed by him, along with all his nobles and all his soldiers. All the Gittites who had followed him from Gath passed before the king.
The king said to Ittai the Gittite, “Why are you going with us too? Stay behind, apart from the king, for you are a foreigner and have also been exiled from your own country.”
You came only yesterday, and today should we make you wander about with us? I am going wherever I can go. Stay and settle your brothers comfortably.
Ittai answered the king, “As the LORD lives, and as you yourself live, O king, wherever my lord the king may be, whether in death or in life, your servant will be there.”
David said to Ittai, “Go on across.” So Ittai the Gittite crossed over, along with all his men and all the families with him.
The whole land wept bitterly as all the people crossed over. The king crossed the Kidron Valley, and all the people crossed over toward the road to the wilderness.
Zadok the priest was also there, with all the Levites who were with him, carrying the ark of God. Abiathar went up until all the people had finished crossing out of the city.
The king said to Zadok, “Take the ark of God back to the city. Perhaps I will find favor in the LORD’s eyes, and he will bring me back and let me see it and its dwelling place.
But if he says, ‘I take no pleasure in you,’ here I stand. Let him do to me whatever seems good to him.”
The king said to Zadok the priest, “Go back to the city in peace, you and your son Ahimaaz, and Nathan son of Abiathar—both your sons with you.
Look, I will wait in the plain of the wilderness until someone comes from you and brings me word.”
So Zadok and Abiathar the priests took the ark of God back to Jerusalem and stayed there.
David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, walking with his head covered. All the people with him covered their heads and went up weeping.
They informed David, saying, “Ahithophel has joined Absalom’s rebellion.” David said, “LORD, thwart Ahithophel’s counsel.”
David reached a certain place where he used to worship God. Hushai the Archite came to him with his tunic torn and dust on his head.
David said to him, “If you cross over with me, you will be a burden to me.
Instead, return to the city and tell Absalom, ‘I am your servant, O king, and have been your father’s servant from long ago.’ And now I, the king, ask you: go and thwart Ahithophel’s counsel.
Zadok and Abiathar the priests are there with you. Tell Zadok and Abiathar the priests everything you hear from the king’s house.
Their two sons are there: Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Nathan son of Abiathar. Send me everything you hear through them.”
So Hushai, David’s friend, went to the city, and Absalom entered Jerusalem.

David had gone a little beyond the place where he used to worship when Ziba, Mephibosheth’s servant, came to meet him. He had with him two loaded donkeys carrying two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred cakes of dried figs, a hundred cheeses, and a skin of wine.

The king said to Ziba, “Where did you get these?” Ziba answered him, “The donkeys are to carry the royal household’s baggage, the bread and cheeses are for the young men to eat, and the wine is for those who become exhausted in the wilderness to drink.”
The king said to him, “Where is your master’s son?” Ziba answered him, “He is staying in Jerusalem, saying, ‘The Israelites will restore to me the kingdom of my father Saul.’”
David said to Ziba, “Everything that belongs to Mephibosheth is given to you.” Ziba said, “I have much, and I have found favor in your eyes, my lord the king.”
King David came as far as Bahurim. A man from the family of Saul’s household came out from there, named Shimei son of Gera. He came out cursing David.
He threw stones at him, at all his servants, at all the people, and at all his servants on his right and on his left.
As Shimei cursed David, he said to him, “Get out! Get out, you bloodshedder and wicked man!

May the Lord repay you for all the blood of Saul’s household, in whose place you became king. May the Lord hand your kingdom over to your son Absalom. Now you have been repaid for your wickedness, because you are a man who sheds blood.”
Abishai son of Zeruiah said to David, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head.”
King David said to him, “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse. The Lord himself told him to curse David. Who, then, says to me, ‘Why [?] like this?’”
David said to Abishai and all his servants, “Look, my son, who came from my own body, seeks to take my life, and now this Benjaminite too! Leave him alone to curse. God himself told him to do it.”
“Perhaps the Lord will look upon my oppression and repay me with good in place of the curses directed at me today.”
David and his servants went along the road, while Shimei went along the hillside opposite him, cursing him, throwing stones at him, and flinging dust at him.
The king and all the people with him arrived exhausted, and they rested there.
Absalom, all the people with him, and all Israel came to Jerusalem, with Ahithophel accompanying him.
When Hushai the Archite, David’s friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, “Long live the king! Long live the king!”
Absalom said to Hushai, “Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?”
Hushai said to Absalom, “No! I belong to the one whom the Lord, these people, and all Israel have chosen, and I will stay with him.”
And I will be his. And secondly, whose servant am I? It was not in my hands [?]. As I served your father, so I will serve you.
Absalom said to Ahithophel, “Advise me. What should I do?”

Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Sleep with your father’s concubines, whom he left to look after his house. When all Israel hears that you have been with your father’s concubines, everyone who is with you will be strengthened.”
They pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof, and Absalom slept with his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel.
In those days, the advice Ahithophel gave was regarded as though someone had consulted the word of God. That was how all Ahithophel’s advice was regarded, both by David and by Absalom.
Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will set out and pursue David during the night.”
I will catch up with him while he is weary and his hands are weak. I will throw him into confusion, and all the people with him will flee. I will kill only the king.
I will bring all the people back to you, as everyone you wanted returns, and all the people will be at peace.
The proposal pleased Absalom and all the elders of Israel.
Absalom said, “Call Hushai the Archite, and let us hear what he has to say as well.”
Hushai came to Absalom, and Absalom said to him, “Ahithophel has said such and such. Should we do what he said? If not, you tell us.”
Hushai said to Absalom, “The advice Ahithophel has given this time is not good.”

Hushai said to him, “You know your father and his servants: they are mighty warriors, and they are embittered men, like a bear bereaved of her cubs in the wilderness. Your father is a man of war, and he will not spend the night beside the people.
Even now he is hiding in one of the locations or in one of the places. When some of them fall at the outset, and word is heard that there has been a slaughter among the people following Absalom,
even a mighty warrior whose heart is like a lion’s heart will utterly lose courage, because all Israel knows that your father is a mighty warrior and that those with him are mighty warriors.
I advise that, when all Israel has gathered to you from Dan as far as Beersheba, you go in their midst.
We will come upon him in whatever place he is found, and descend upon him as dew falls on the ground. Neither he nor a single one of all the men with him will remain.
If he enters a town, all Israel will bring ropes to it, and they will drag it down to the valley. We will not leave even a pebble there.

Absalom and all Israel said, “The advice of Hushai the Archite is better than the advice of Ahithophel.” The Lord had commanded that Ahithophel’s good advice be frustrated, so that the Lord might bring disaster upon Absalom.
Hushai said to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, “Ahithophel advised Absalom and all Israel in such and such a way, and I advised them in such and such a way.
Now send word quickly to David and tell him, ‘Do not spend the night in the wilderness plain. Cross over, so that you and all the people with you will not perish.’”
Nathan and Ahimaaz were standing beside the Fuller’s Spring. A servant girl went and informed them, and they went and informed King David, because they could not be seen entering the city.
But a young man saw them and informed Absalom. The two of them went and entered the house of a man from Bahurim. He had a well in his courtyard, and they climbed down into it.
The woman took a covering and spread it over the well, and spread crushed grain on it. No one knew about it.

Absalom’s servants came to the woman’s house and said, “Where are Ahimaaz and Nathan?” The woman told them, “They have gone on from here because of the water.” They searched but did not find them, and returned to Jerusalem.
After they had gone, the two men climbed out of the well and went and informed King David. They told him, “Get up quickly and cross the water, because Ahithophel has advised this against you.”
David and all the people with him got up and crossed the Jordan. By dawn, not one person remained who had not crossed the Jordan.

When Ahithophel saw that his advice had not been adopted, he saddled his donkey and set out for his home in his own town. He put his household affairs in order, hanged himself, and died. He was buried in his father’s tomb.
David crossed over to Mahanaim, and Absalom crossed the Jordan with all Israel.
Absalom appointed Amasa over the army in place of Joab. Amasa was the son of an Israelite man named Ithra, who had slept with Abigail, the daughter of Nahash and sister of Zeruiah, Joab’s mother.
Israel and Absalom camped in the land of Gilead.
When David came to Mahanaim, Abishai son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, Machir son of Gamiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Doblin
brought beds, bedding, pottery vessels, wheat, barley, roasted grain, flour, beans, and lentils.
They also brought honey, butter, sheep, and cheese made from cows’ milk for David and the people with him to eat, because they said, “The people are hungry, exhausted, and thirsty in the wilderness.”
David counted the people with him and appointed commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds over them.
A third were with Joab, a third with Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, and a third with Ittai the Gittite. The king said to the people,

“If we flee, they will pay no attention to us. Now ten thousand are enough for us. It is better for us to have helpers from the towns.” David’s servants said to him, “We will go out and hurry to fight them.”
The king told them, “Do whatever seems right to you.” The king stood beside the gate, and all the people went out in hundreds and thousands.
The king commanded Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, “Capture the young man Absalom alive for me.” All the people heard the king giving orders to all the commanders concerning Absalom.
The people went out into the open country to meet Israel, and the battle began.
The people of Israel were defeated there by David’s servants, and there was a great slaughter there: twenty thousand.
The battle spread fiercely over the land, and the wild animals of the forest devoured more of the people than the sword destroyed that day.

Absalom came upon David’s servants. Absalom was riding a mule, and the mule went under the branches of a great oak. Absalom’s head became caught in the great oak, and he was left hanging between heaven and earth, while the mule beneath him went on.
A man saw him and told Joab, saying, “I saw Absalom hanging in an oak.”
Joab said to the man who told him, “When you saw him, why did you not strike him down to the ground? I would have given you ten pieces of silver and a garment.”

The man said to Joab, “Even if you had counted out and given me a thousand pieces of silver, I would not have raised my hand against the king’s son. For in my presence the king commanded you, Abishai, and Ittai, saying, ‘For my sake, take care of the young man Absalom.’”
“If I had acted on my own, I would have been guilty. Nothing would have been hidden from the king, and you would have stood against me.”
Joab said to him, “I will not linger here with you like this.” Joab took three shafts in his hand and thrust them into Absalom’s heart while he was still alive, hanging in the oak.
Then ten young men who carried Joab’s weapons turned on Absalom, struck him, and killed him.
Joab sounded the trumpet, and the troops who had been pursuing Israel turned back, because Joab restrained the troops.
They took Absalom and threw him into a pit, a great hollow, and raised over him a great heap of large stones. All Israel fled, each to his own tent.

While Absalom was still alive, he had set up a monument for himself in the Valley of the Kings, because he said, “I have no one to preserve my name.” He named the monument after himself, and it is called Absalom’s Monument to this day.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok said, “Let me run and bring the king the good news that the Lord has vindicated him against his enemies.”
Joab said to him, “You should not bring news today. Bring news another day, but do not bring news today, for you would be announcing that the king’s son is dead.”
Joab said to the Cushite, “Go, tell the king what you have seen.”

Ahimaaz son of Zadok again ran up and said to Joab, “Whatever happens, let me also run and go after the Cushite.” Joab said to him, “Why should you run, my son, when no one will give you a reward for the news?”
He said to him, “Whatever happens, let me run.” He said to him, “Run.” So Ahimaaz ran by the road through the plain and overtook the Cushite.
David was sitting between the two gates. The watchman went up onto the roof of the gate in the wall, looked up, and saw a man running alone.
The watchman called out and told the king. The king said, “If he is alone, he has news to tell.” The man kept coming closer.
The watchman called toward the gate and said, “Look, another man is running alone!”
The watchman said, “I see that the first man runs like Ahimaaz son of Zadok.” The king said, “He is a good man, and he comes with good news.”

He called to Ahimaaz, and the king said to him, “You have arrived safely.” Ahimaaz bowed facedown to the ground before the king and said, “Blessed be the Lord your God, who has handed over the men who raised their hands against my lord the king!”

The king said to him, “Is the young man Absalom safe?” Ahimaaz said to him, “I saw a great force drawn up against Joab, the servant of my lord the king, and against your servant. I did not know what it was.”
The king said to him, “Stand here.” So he turned aside and stood there.
Then the Cushite arrived and said, “Let my lord the king receive good news, for today the Lord has vindicated him against all who rose against him.”
The king said to the Cushite, “Is the young man Absalom safe?” The Cushite said, “May your enemies, my lord the king, and all who have risen against you to harm you, be like that young man.”
The king was deeply distressed and went up to the chamber and wept. As he wept, he kept saying, “My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you, Absalom, my son!”
Joab was told, “The king is weeping and mourning for Absalom.”
That day became a day of mourning for all the people, because the people heard that day that the king was grieving over his son.
The people slipped into the city that day as people slip away in shame when they flee from battle.
The king covered his face and cried out loudly, saying, “My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom!”
Joab went in to the king and said to him, “Today you have shamed all your servants, who today saved your life and the lives of your sons and daughters, your wives, and your concubines.

You have loved those who hate you and hated those who love you. Today you have shown that neither nobles nor servants mean anything to you. I know today that if Absalom were alive and we were all dead, you would be pleased.

Now get up, go out, and speak to your servants. For I swear by the Lord that if you do not go out, not one person will stay with you tonight. This will be worse for you than all the troubles that have come upon you from your youth until now.”

The king got up and sat at the gate. All the people were told, “Look, the king is sitting at the gate.” Then all the people came before the king. Meanwhile, the Israelites had fled, each to his own tent.

All the people throughout all the tribes of Israel were debating and saying, “The king rescued us from the power of all our enemies, and he saved us from the power of the Philistines. Now come, let us flee from the land after Absalom.
For Absalom, whom we anointed and appointed over us, has died in battle.” They said to one another, “Why, then, are you now hesitating to return with the king?”
Come, let us bring him back to his home.” The words of all the Israelites reached the king.
He said to them, “You are my brothers, my own flesh and bone. Why have you been the last to return with the king?”
He said to Amasa, “Look, you are my own flesh and bone. May God do this to me, and more besides, if you do not become commander of the army before me for all time in place of Joab.”
He won over the hearts of everyone in the house of Judah as one man. They sent word to the king, saying, “Return, you and all your servants.”
The king returned and came as far as the Jordan. The people of Judah came to Gilgal to go and meet the king and bring him across the Jordan.
Shimei son of Gera, a Benjaminite, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
Ziba, Saul’s servant, with his fifteen sons and his twenty servants, crossed over and bridged the Jordan before the king.
They made crossings to bring the king’s household across and to do whatever pleased him. Shimei son of Gera fell down before the king as he crossed the Jordan.

He said to the king, “My lord, do not hold my offense against me, and do not remember the wrong your servant did on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. Let my lord the king put it out of his mind.
I, your servant, know that I have sinned. Look, today I have come first out of all the house of Joseph and have come down to meet my lord the king.”
Abishai son of Zeruiah answered, “Should Shimei not be put to death for this, because he cursed the Lord’s anointed?”
David said, “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah, that you should oppose me today? No one in Israel will be put to death today. Do I not know today that I am king over Israel?”
The king said to Shimei, “You will not die.” And the king swore an oath to him.
Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came down to meet the king. He had neither trimmed his beard nor changed his clothes from the day the king left until the day the king returned safely.
When he came to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, “Mephibosheth, why did you not go with me?”
Mephibosheth said to him, “My lord the king, my servant deceived me. For I told him, ‘Put me on the donkey so that I can ride it and go with my lord the king,’ because your servant is lame.
My servant told lies about me, my lord the king. But you, my lord the king, are like an angel of God. Do whatever seems right to you.

For my father's entire household deserved death at your hands, my lord the king, yet you counted your servant among those who eat at your table. Now I cannot claim any right or even speak before my lord the king.
The king said to him, “You have said enough. I have decided that you and Ziba are to divide the fields.”
Mephibosheth said to the king, “Let the servant take it all, now that my lord the king has come home safely.”
Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Doblin and crossed the Jordan with the king to see him off from there.
Barzillai was very old, eighty years old. He had provided for the king while he was staying at Mahanaim, for he was a wealthy man.
The king said to Barzillai, “You too, cross over with me, and I will provide for you with me in Jerusalem.”
Barzillai said to the king, “How many years of life do I have left, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?

I am eighty years old today, and I cannot distinguish good from bad. Your servant cannot taste what he eats or drinks. Nor can I any longer hear the voice of one woman or another. Why should your servant be a further burden to my lord the king?
Your servant can barely cross the Jordan with my lord the king. Let my lord the king not repay me with this reward.

Let your servant remain, so that I may die in my own town beside the grave of my father and mother. Here with you is your servant, my son Chimham. Let him cross over with you, my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you.”
The king said, “Chimham shall cross over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to me. Whatever you ask of me, I will do for you.”
All the people crossed the Jordan, and the king also crossed. The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai returned to his own place.
The king crossed over to Gilgal, and Chimham crossed over with him. All the people of Judah crossed over with the king, and also half the people of Israel.

All Israel came to the king and said to him, “Why did our brothers, the men of Judah, take you away secretly and bring you across the Jordan—you, the king, all your household, and all those of the house of Judah with you?”

All the people of Judah answered the people of Israel, “Because the king is closely related to us. Why are you upset about this? Have we eaten anything at the king's expense, or has he given us a gift?”

The people of Israel answered the people of Judah, “We have ten shares in the king, and we have more of a share in David than you do. Why have you treated us with contempt? We should have been the first to bring the king back.” But the words of the people of Judah were harsher than those of the people of Israel.

Now a wicked man happened to be there, named Shammua son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. He blew the trumpet and said, “We have no share in David and no inheritance in the son of Jesse. Go, everyone, to your own tent!”
All the Israelites stopped following David and followed Shammua son of Bichri. But the people of Judah stayed with their king from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

David came to his house in Jerusalem. The king took the ten concubines whom he had left to look after his house and confined them in a house under guard. He provided for them but did not have sexual relations with them. They remained in distress until the day he died, and lived as widows.
The king said to Amasa, “Summon the people of Judah for me within three days, and you remain here.”
Amasa went to summon the people of Judah, but he delayed beyond the time appointed for him.

David said to Joab, “Now Shammua son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your master's servants with you and pursue him, or he may find fortified towns for himself, establish himself in them, and gouge out our eyes.”
Joab's companions, the nobles, the soldiers, and all the men went out after him. They left Jerusalem and pursued Shammua son of Bichri.

They reached the great rock at Gibeon, and Amasa came before them. Joab was dressed in his battle gear, with a sword fastened at his waist like a razor. As he went forward, his hand fell upon his sword.
Joab said to Amasa, “Peace to you, my brother!” Joab's hand took hold of Amasa's beard, and he kissed him.

Amasa did not watch out for the sword in Joab's hand. Joab struck him with it in the abdomen, and his intestines spilled onto the ground. He did not strike him a second time, and he died. Joab and his brother Abishai pursued Shammua son of Bichri.
One of Joab's servants went and stood over him and said to him, “Whose side are you on? David's? Follow Joab!”

Amasa was wallowing in his blood, lying in the road. When the man saw that all the people were stopping to look, he dragged Amasa out of the road and threw him into a field. He threw a rag over him, because he saw that everyone who passed him stopped.
When he had dragged him out of the road, everyone went on after Joab. They pursued Shammua son of Bichri to attack him.
They passed through all the tribes of Israel, through Abel and Beth-maacah and all the Berites, and went after him.
They came and encamped against him at Abel and Beth-maacah. They laid ambushes against the town, and it was in distress. All the people with Joab were eager to bring down the wall.
A wise woman called from the wall, saying, “Listen! Listen! Tell Joab, ‘Come here so that I can speak to you.’”
He approached her, and she said to him, “Are you Joab?” He said to her, “I am.” She said to him, “Listen to the words of your servant.” He said, “I am listening.”
The woman said, “Long ago people used to say, ‘They would consult the prophets, and only then destroy.’
“I am one who makes good Israel’s losses. You seek to kill a child and its mother in Israel, to swallow up the LORD’s inheritance.”
Joab answered her, “Far be it from me! I will neither swallow up nor destroy.

“That is not the case. Rather, a man from the hill country of Ephraim, named Shammua son of Bichri, has raised his hands against King David. Hand over that man alone to me, and I will withdraw from the town.” The woman said to Joab, “His head will now be thrown to you from the wall.”

The woman went to all the people in her wisdom. They cut off the head of Shammua son of Bichri and threw it from the wall to Joab. Joab sounded the trumpet, and they withdrew from the town, each going to his tent. Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.
Joab was over the whole army of Israel, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the nobles and the soldiers.
Adoniram was in charge of the tribute, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder.
Seraiah was the scribe, and Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
Aza from Jattir was also David’s priest.
